comments.text:
Writing this down so I remember it better.

1. Pay the effort, not outcome. "I showed up." Stop attaching reward to results. 
2. Move reward to the doorway. Attach a treat to when you do something specific (ex. audiobook only at the gym).
3. Shrink entry point until resisting is absurd
. Start with tiny baby steps. Repetition is the key. Small is repeatable. It's ok to make mistakes here and there -- stumbling isn't an issue, it's falling and never getting back up that is the end.
4. Design the room, not your resolve. Eliminate temptations instead of constantly fighting them. Plan & do this when you feel fine/things are still easy. 
5. Never end on failure. Deliberately end on something that is good. Even a tiny win. Your brain will remember it. 

Basically, learn to love the process. Train your nervous system to work with you as an ally. The journey is the goal.

comments.text:
Most of us were raised in a culture that believes discipline equals self-punishment. If we can't get out of bed at 6 AM, we call ourselves lazy or weak. But neuroscience tells a completely different, mind-blowing story. Our brain's cost-benefit center (the dACC) is constantly running the numbers. When you force yourself to do something while constantly criticizing and hating yourself, you are literally teaching your nervous system that "effort = punishment." It's called backward conditioning.

Your brain isn't broken or lazy when it paralyzes you before a task; it's actually just trying to protect you from the toxic stress you've associated with hard work. We are basically giving ourselves "Learned Helplessness." The goal isn't to build more willpower to fight yourself or beat yourself up even harder. The goal is to rewire your brain to stop seeing effort as a threat. Treat your brain like a machine, not a moral courtroom. Stop the self-hate, and start the system reboot. Brilliant video.

For me, I’m best at (4) Designing the Room, then have become increasingly better at (3) shrinking the entry for the past years. The hardest part about 2 is remembering that “the people who failed are the people who quit- not the people who slipped.” because I have subconsciously attached the concept of consistency with unbroken streaks. 
My Missing Pieces are:

1. PAYING THE EFFORT (for the exact childhood reasons mentioned)
- REWRITING PREDICTION!!
-rewarding showing up and THE ACT (tick the box when I start & say “I showed up”) instead of outcomes/results and rewriting the internal “Finally! well, thats the least you can do. Now, let’s see you finish”
- recategorizing effort as pure cost!
- the rewarding mediocrity and reminding myself that I’m not evaluating performance is formidable. I can feel my internal council jumping at this one every time I listen to this concept. 😊 

2. Moving the Reward to the entry - not exit!

5. Ending on wins, even tiny ones! (final 30s). My internal Council is working towards aligning my nervous system with positive anticipation instead of force and self-criticism.

comments.text:
In addition to these, which are excellent, lie to yourself. Say you like the thing you're having trouble doing. Constantly. Tell other people you like it. 
I did this a few years ago with math and exercising. It sounds insane but I actually genuinely enjoy sitting down with a difficult math problem. I enjoy being sore. Learning to do, and enjoy, the difficult things will absolutely change your life.
